## Codex automated review

Reviewed commit `6e7498c8a506` with the official Codex CLI.

The continuum path reads an uninitialized optional output and inconsistently handles shifted-energy recovery. Tests could not be executed because pytest and a Fortran compiler are unavailable; native lifetime and bounds-check evidence remains unverified.

Full review comments:

- [P2] Avoid reading augmentation coefficients when augmentation is disabled — /var/lib/codex-review/work/project-19-mr-1/source/spec/pecd_bs_ccsolve.f90:372-372
  With the default `mc=0`, `pecd_bspline_run` allocates and passes `yA`, but `cc_solve_once` only initializes it through `mc_schur` when `mc%active` is true. This unconditional scaling therefore reads undefined values on ordinary single-centre runs and can trigger floating-point exceptions in diagnostic builds. Guard the scaling on active augmentation or initialize the inactive output. This violates the initialization requirement in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#L172-L174).

- [P2] Propagate the actual energy used by a successful retry — /var/lib/codex-review/work/project-19-mr-1/source/spec/pecd_bs_ccsolve.f90:234-239
  When the initial solve fails and a shifted-energy retry succeeds, the returned continuum and Coulomb phases correspond to `Es`, but `pecd_bspline_run` still uses the original energy for `k`, dipole normalization, photon energy, and the persisted energy coordinate. The resulting cross section mixes two energies and is reported at a point that was never successfully solved, particularly problematic near resonances. Either retain the requested physical energy during recovery or return and consistently use the effective energy.

## Rule 4 closed: companion documentation merge request

[openqp-docs!1](https://qchemlab.knu.ac.kr/open-quantum-platform/openqp-docs/-/merge_requests/1)
is open and linked from this merge request's description.

- `docs/keywords/pecd.md`, new. It leads with the choice of engine, because that
  decides both the cost and whether the number carries an absolute scale, and it
  states the muffin-tin restriction that makes `engine=0` refuse the common case
  of an emission centre sitting on a heavy atom. Every keyword says which engine
  uses it, including the `mc` augmentation added in the previous round.
- `docs/keywords/ekt.md`, extended with `photon_energy`, `population`,
  `core_threshold` and `renormalize`, together with the reason the Gelius model
  exists at all: EKT pole strengths are close to one for every retained root of
  a closed-shell ground state, so they carry no information about how channels
  compare.
- `mkdocs.yml`, `pecd` wired into the keywords nav after `ekt`.

Checked rather than assumed: every keyword in the `[pecd]` and `[ekt]` schemas
is documented and no documented keyword is absent from the code (17 and 6
respectively); every page in the nav exists; the cross-links between the two
pages resolve; and the worked input on the `pecd` page was extracted from the
rendered markdown verbatim and run, giving `mc=1` and cross sections of 4.82 and
6.62 Mb at 5 and 10 eV.

That leaves rule 7's repeated-call and error-path lifetime evidence as the only
gate I have not satisfied, and I have not claimed otherwise in any round.

## Codex automated review

Reviewed commit `b305c4608b27` with the official Codex CLI.

The multicentre engine has an out-of-bounds access for accepted angular cutoffs. Rule 1's registration check passes; rules 2, 3, 5 and 6 have examples, API tests, devkit separation and spherical regressions. The rule 4 companion-documentation link could not be verified, and rule 7 native bounds/lifetime verification remains incomplete because the compiler and pytest are unavailable.

Review comment:

- [P2] Size multicentre angular tables for both angular cutoffs — /var/lib/codex-review/work/project-19-mr-1/source/spec/pecd_mc.f90:520-524
  With `engine=1`, `mc=1`, `lmax=1` and the default `mc_lmax=2`, an augmented centre on the expansion z-axis reaches `Tmm(fm_of(f), fm_of(g))` with first indices ±2, although this allocation only permits ±1. This reads outside the array and corrupts the atom-centred Hamiltonian or aborts under bounds checking. Larger `mc_lmax` values also exceed `azb`'s bounds. Size and populate these tables for both angular cutoffs, or reject unsupported combinations before assembly, and add a bounds-checked regression as required by [AGENTS.md:186–189](AGENTS.md#L186-L189).

## Seventh review response (`b305c460`)

Covers both reviews, `561f0276` and `df6b69a1`. Three confirmed and fixed; the
P1 does not reproduce and I give the measurement below. One of the fixes
invalidates a conclusion I had recorded elsewhere, which is the most important
thing in this round.

### [P2] Recompute the matrix norm after equilibration — confirmed, and it mattered

`anorm` came from `fill_banded`, i.e. from A before the symmetric diagonal
equilibration, while `dgbcon` was handed the LU factors of `D A D`. It is now
computed on the equilibrated band before factorization.

The consequence is larger than a wrong diagnostic. For N2/6-31G* the reported
rcond goes from **8.18e-24 to 1.28e-10** — fourteen orders of magnitude, and the
true value is unremarkable. `dg%fallback` triggers below 1e-12, so that flag was
being raised at every energy too, exactly as you said.

Cross sections are bit-identical, because the fallback is report-only today. But
the old numbers had been used for something: `devkit/docs/pecd_continuum_handoff.md`
listed solver conditioning as the remaining suspect for thymine's `lmax`
non-convergence, on the strength of "rcond ~1e-23". That conclusion rested
entirely on this artefact. The document is corrected in this commit and the
conditioning hypothesis is withdrawn.

### [P2] Example exercising multicentre augmentation — confirmed

It was opt-in through `OQP_PECD_MC` only, so no input file could turn it on and
nothing in the repository exercised the separate potential correction, augmented
basis, Schur solve or dipole contribution. An environment variable is not a
reproducible invocation, so rather than add an example that exports one, the
augmentation is now an ordinary keyword: `[pecd] mc`, `mc_lmax`, `mc_nseg`, with
the environment variables kept as an override for scripted scans. The engine
reports the mode it was given, `examples/other/h2o_rohf_mrsf_ekt_ip_pecd_bspline_mc_6-31gs.inp`
drives it, and a native regression asserts on it.

### [P2] Reject nonpositive photoelectron energies — confirmed

`energies=0,10` was forwarded unchecked although `k = sqrt(2E)` goes straight
into the spherical Bessel and Coulomb functions. Entries must now be finite and
strictly positive, and the error names the offending values.

### [P1] Unconditional REAL128 — not reproduced

The premise does not hold for the supported toolchains, and I checked rather
than argued:

    $ /opt/homebrew/bin/gfortran-15 ...   # Apple Silicon, arm64
     selected_real_kind(30) =  16
     real128 kind =           16
     b =  0.333333333333333333333333333333333317

33 significant digits. This arm64 host has been building this file all session,
and the `macos-arm64-accelerate-ilp64` CI leg passed on `df6b69a1`, the very
commit under review.

I have not changed the arithmetic, and I want to be explicit about why rather
than appear to ignore the finding. The quad precision is what stops the
alternating Racah sum in `wigner_3j` from losing every correct digit beyond
l ~ 20; that cancellation is the bug it was introduced to fix, and `lmax >= 20`
runs aborted before it. Substituting real64 would reinstate that silently, so
there is no "numerically suitable alternative" in double precision to offer. If
a toolchain without REAL128 ever has to be supported, the real substitute is a
log-gamma formulation of the Racah sum or double-double arithmetic.

What the finding does justify is a readable failure. The module now states the
requirement and carries a named parameter, so such a toolchain stops there
instead of emitting `real(-1)` errors from every routine.

### A mistake worth recording

Adding the keyword needed the C struct in `include/oqp.h` as well as the Fortran
`bind(c)` type. I updated only the Fortran side first, and the two new tests
failed. The instructive part: the engine-0 regression's `returncode != 0`
assertion **passed for the wrong reason** — the run died in input setup, long
before reaching the engine — and only the assertion on the message caught it.
An exit-code check alone would have gone green on a completely broken build.

### Verification

Build clean, three no-LP64-leak checks. 38 tests pass. All three examples run
(`mc=0` and `mc=1` both reported). The engine-1 N2/6-31G* baseline is
bit-identical, so nothing the manuscript depends on moved.

Rule 4 remains unmet and is with the author: this adds user-facing keywords and
no openqp-docs merge request exists. Rule 7's repeated-call and error-path
lifetime evidence still has not been produced.

## Codex automated review

Reviewed commit `df6b69a1a8e6` with the official Codex CLI.

The patch introduces a macOS ARM compilation failure and accepts energy grids outside the continuum solvers' domain. Rules 1 and 5 gates pass; examples and API tests address rules 2–3, and spherical tests accompany rule 6. The companion documentation link (rule 4) and lifetime evidence (rule 7) remain unverified; numerical tests could not run because pytest and a Fortran compiler are unavailable.

Full review comments:

- [P1] Provide a portable alternative to unconditional REAL128 arithmetic — /var/lib/codex-review/work/project-19-mr-1/source/spec/pecd_special.f90:33-36
  On Apple Silicon, the supported Homebrew gfortran toolchain does not provide REAL128, so `qp` is negative and the new `real(qp)` declarations and `_qp` literals fail compilation. Unlike the existing unused QP constant in `precision.F90`, this module actually instantiates quadruple-precision arithmetic. Since the spectroscopy sources are compiled unconditionally, this breaks the entire macOS ARM build, even without PECD enabled. Detect support and provide a numerically suitable alternative.

- [P2] Reject nonpositive photoelectron energies before native execution — /var/lib/codex-review/work/project-19-mr-1/pyoqp/oqp/molecule/oqpdata.py:1660-1663
  A grid such as `[pecd] energies=0,10` is accepted and forwarded without validation, but both continuum engines require strictly positive kinetic energies. Zero produces divisions by zero in the spherical-Bessel or Coulomb calculations, while negative energies produce invalid square roots; engine 1 can spend substantial time assembling its operators before exposing failed results. Validate that every nonempty grid entry is finite and strictly positive before invoking the native engine.

## Sixth review response (`df6b69a1`)

Both confirmed and fixed. On the first one the location is right but the
mechanism is worse than described, and I have a correction to make about rule 4
that I got wrong in my previous two responses.

### [P2] Scattering at a coincident emission centre — confirmed, worse than stated

The branch you name needs agreement to **1e-12 a0** and so never fires on a real
molecule. What actually happens is not suppression. These are KKR site-to-site
structure constants built from outgoing Hankel functions that grow as
`(kR)^-(l''+1)`, and they are defined only between separated sites. With the
emitter merely *near* an atom they are evaluated at a tiny separation and
dominate everything else while staying finite, so the run completes and reports
plausible numbers.

Measured, water/cc-pVDZ, 1b1 channel: the Dyson centroid sits **0.005 a0** from
the oxygen, giving `|h_6(kR)| ~ 4e20` against `~5e2` for the hydrogens. Eighteen
orders of magnitude, silently.

The real precondition is that the emission centre lies outside every scatterer's
muffin-tin sphere. That is now checked before any coupling is built, and a
contained emitter is refused, naming the scatterer, its distance and its
muffin-tin radius, and pointing at `engine=1`. `build_G` aborts on a zero
displacement instead of returning a zero coupling, because a zero structure
constant is never the right answer.

Two consequences you should weigh, since they go past the finding:

1. This makes engine 0, **the default**, refuse geometries it previously
   answered — water among them, and any molecule whose Dyson centroid sits on a
   heavy atom, which is the common case.
2. Engine 0 disagrees with engine 1 even when no atom is near the centre. Its
   `b2` is nearly energy-independent: water 0.0749 / 0.0745 / 0.0734 and N2
   -0.3468 / -0.3451 / -0.3489 at 5 / 10 / 20 eV, against engine 1's
   -0.502 / -0.665 / -0.776 and -0.488 / -0.366 / -0.256.

So the coincident emitter is one symptom rather than the whole story, and
whether engine 0 should stay the default is a maintainer decision I have not
made on my own.

### [P2] Arbitrary intensity exposed as a cross section — confirmed, my regression

`get_pecd_results` documented `'sigma'` as Mb for both engines while the
tagarray description for engine 0 already said "arbitrary units, no absolute
scale". That contract came from my own change in the round that made engine 0
persist its results. The getter now returns `'engine'` and `'sigma_units'`
(`'Mb'` for engine 1, `'arbitrary'` for engine 0) and the docstring says the two
must not be compared.

### Correction: rule 4 is not satisfied, and my previous answer was wrong

In my fourth and fifth responses I said rule 4's documentation lived in the
openqp-devkit handoff and could not be resolved across repositories. That was
wrong. Rule 4 is about
[open-quantum-platform/openqp-docs](https://qchemlab.knu.ac.kr/open-quantum-platform/openqp-docs),
the user manual: a keyword page under `docs/keywords/` and/or a workflow page
under `docs/workflows/`, wired into `mkdocs.yml`, with the companion merge
request linked from this description. The devkit handoff is developer material
and belongs to rule 5, not rule 4.

This merge request adds user-facing keywords - the whole `[pecd]` section and
the Gelius keywords on `[ekt]` - so rule 4 genuinely applies and is **not**
met. No openqp-docs merge request exists yet. I am raising it with the author
rather than quietly opening one in another repository.

### Note on the devkit merge

Internal `main` moved to `d8fcc411` while this round was in flight, bringing the
devkit back in. This branch is merged up to it. `devkit/docs/pecd_continuum_handoff.md`
now lives in this repository, so that document at least is resolvable from here,
even though it is rule 5 material rather than rule 4.

### Verification

Build clean, three no-LP64-leak checks. 36 tests pass. The engine-1 N2/6-31G*
baseline is bit-identical, so nothing that depends on engine 1 moved.

The new regression runs **out of process**: the refusal goes through the Fortran
abort path, which terminates rather than raising, so an in-process
`pytest.raises` took the whole test session down without reporting anything.
That is how I found it, and it is worth knowing for any future test of an abort
path in this codebase.

Rule 7's repeated-call and error-path lifetime evidence still has not been
produced.

## Codex automated review

Reviewed commit `d395f5db8108` with the official Codex CLI.

The default continuum engine suppresses scattering at a coincident emission centre, and its arbitrary intensities are exposed as absolute cross sections. The BLAS registration check passed; native and pytest validation were unavailable in this environment.

Full review comments:

- [P2] Preserve scattering from an atom at the emission centre — /var/lib/codex-review/work/project-19-mr-1/source/spec/pecd_cmsxalpha.f90:66-68
  When the Dyson centroid coincides with an atom, this branch sets both its primary-to-atom and atom-to-primary coupling matrices to zero. Consequently, `scatter_and_assemble` completely removes that atom's scattering contribution; for a single atom, engine 0 returns the free-wave dipole regardless of its potential or phase shifts. Handle the coincident emitter with an appropriate local scattering contribution rather than suppressing it.

- [P2] Distinguish arbitrary intensity from cross sections in the API — /var/lib/codex-review/work/project-19-mr-1/pyoqp/oqp/molecule/molecule.py:2193-2195
  For the default `engine=0`, `pecd_run` explicitly stores an arbitrarily scaled dipole intensity in `OQP_pecd_sigma`, but this public getter labels it as a cross section in Mb and returns no engine or unit information. Users therefore receive values that cannot be compared with engine 1's absolute cross sections despite an identical API contract. Return explicit units/normalization metadata or expose the engine-0 quantity under a distinct intensity key.

## Fifth review response (`d395f5db`)

Confirmed and fixed. This is a genuinely separate site from the one in the
previous round, and you were right that my test could not see it. One part of
the finding does not survive measurement, and I give the numbers below.

### [P2] Angular factors in the tight Dyson projection — confirmed

The Dyson channel projection has its own tight/smooth split, independent of the
density split I fixed last round. The smooth copy zeroed every primitive above
exponent 25 and the analytic block added them all back with the displaced
spherical-Gaussian identity, which is an identity for `exp(-z|r-d|^2)` and
nothing else. A tight p primitive was removed as a p and reinserted as an s.
Both comments in the file already read "tight s-primitives"; neither filter ever
tested the angular momentum.

Fixed the way you suggested first: the analytic path now admits s primitives
only, which is exactly what that identity covers, and tight non-s primitives
stay in the numerical projection. That projection resolves them unless they
alias the angular grid, so the engine now computes `sqrt(2*zeta)*|d - centre|`
and reports it, warning when it exceeds `lmax_d` instead of returning a silently
wrong orbital.

### The diagnostics were blind to that path, which is the deeper problem

You noted my test checked only positivity and the smooth-part norm. That was not
just a weak test: the captured norm and the per-l norms were **accumulated from
the smooth part only**, while the analytic contribution went straight into
`rhs`. No test could have seen this path, and the reassuring 0.999809 I quoted
last round was measuring the half of the orbital that was never in question.
The tight-s terms are now added to the same `P_c(r)` before it is squared, so
both diagnostics describe the whole orbital.

### [rule 6] Symmetry regression — added

Water lies in the yz plane, so root 5 is the out-of-plane 1b1 lone pair, odd
under x -> -x about a centre that symmetry pins to x = 0. Every channel even in
x must vanish, l = 0 most cleanly, and it needs no reference value.

    cc-pVDZ   l=0  9.4156E-30    l=1  1.0004
    cc-pVTZ   l=0  3.5168E-29    l=1  1.0004

Admitting a p primitive to the tight-s path deposits l = 0 amplitude and breaks
this immediately, while leaving the cross section looking plausible - which is
what made the earlier checks useless here.

### Scale of the defect: smaller than the review states

I measured it rather than assume, and the consequence is not what the finding
claims. Water/cc-pVTZ cross sections change by **3e-5 relative**
(7.62846 -> 7.62872 Mb at 10 eV), not corrupted cross sections and dichroism.
The reason is in the new diagnostic: that oxygen p primitive sits essentially on
the expansion centre, `L_eff = 0.05`, so it never aliased anything, and it
carries little weight in the 1b1 orbital.

What it did do is misplace **0.37% of the Dyson norm**: `norm_l(1)` goes
0.99674 -> 1.00040. That is a real defect in a conserved quantity and worth
fixing on its own terms, and the error grows with the primitive's distance from
the centroid, which is what the aliasing report now covers. But on the case the
finding names, the effect on the reported observables is five orders of
magnitude smaller than "corrupting the Dyson orbital and resulting cross
sections".

### Verification

Build clean, three no-LP64-leak checks. 35 tests pass: 9 native spherical plus
the 26 EKT/photoionization ones. cc-pVDZ is bit-identical before and after, and
so is the N2/6-31G* baseline these manuscript numbers rest on, since neither
basis contains a tight non-s primitive - only cc-pVTZ and larger do.

Two of my own test assertions failed on the first run, both too loose rather
than wrong code: one matched the abort string as a substring of the new
informational line, the other rejected any "WARNING" in a log that also carries
an unrelated MRSF symmetry-block warning. Both are now specific.

On the remaining gates: rule 4's documentation link is in openqp-devkit, which
the user is re-merging; I will verify the link resolves once that lands. Rule 7
repeated-call and error-path lifetime evidence still has not been produced, and
I would rather keep saying so than imply coverage I have not run.

## Fourth review response (`f708d5f9`)

All three confirmed and fixed. The first one turned out to be the visible half
of a defect that was affecting every basis, so thank you for it.

### [P2] Tight non-s primitives — confirmed, and it hid a second defect

You are right that cc-pVTZ aborts. I checked the shipped bases: 6-31G* tops out
at p = 15.54 and cc-pVDZ at 17.70, both under the cutoff of 25, which is why no
existing test or example ever reached this line. cc-pVTZ oxygen is 34.46 and
nitrogen 26.63; cc-pV5Z reaches 195.5.

While fixing it I found that the same lines had a quieter problem. The guard
tested the angular momentum of the **tight** primitive only, but a pair is
retained when **either** member is tight. So every (tight s) x (smooth p) pair
passed the guard and was still collapsed to a single point charge at the product
centre, discarding a dipole the s*s argument never covered. N2/6-31G* has 32
such pairs and has never aborted, so this was live in every result the engine
has produced.

Both are fixed the same way. A retained pair is now represented by point charges
that reproduce its charge **and** its dipole about P exactly: one charge
displaced to the charge centroid when the monopole can carry the dipole over a
short distance, otherwise a +/- pair straddling P (an odd pair has zero
monopole, so the single-charge form does not exist for it). An s*s pair has no
dipole about P and keeps its previous single charge bit for bit. What remains is
the intrinsic quadrupole of a tight Gaussian, O(1/gam) < 0.04 a0^2. This adds
`prim_dipole_P` and generalises `s1d` to an arbitrary Hermite order.

The N2 regression moves by 7e-5 relative (10.417607 -> 10.416875 Mb at the
resonance). That difference is exactly the dipole term that was being thrown
away.

### [P2] Residual ionic charge — confirmed

`1.0_dp` went to both `vpot_build` and `cc_solve`, so for a charged molecule the
imposed Coulomb tail and the Coulomb functions the solution is matched to were
both wrong, with no diagnostic. It is now derived once as
`infos%mol_prop%charge + 1` and printed. Water at charge +2 reports `Zion = 3.0`
and gives a visibly different continuum (6.39 -> 2.33 Mb at 10 eV), so this is a
real change of the solved problem and not only a label.

### [P2] High angular momentum population bins — confirmed

`gross_populations` allocated `lmax+1 = 5` bins and the sole caller never
overrode `lmax`, so `ao_l = 5` from a cc-pV5Z h shell indexed past the end. The
bin count now comes from the basis. Checked directly: the previous build raises
`IndexError: index 5 is out of bounds for axis 2 with size 5` on an AO set
containing an h function, and this one bins it and routes the population to the
existing dropped-population path.

### [rule 6] cc-pVTZ coverage — added

`tests/test_pecd_spherical_basis.py` now runs cc-pVTZ as well as cc-pVDZ, so it
reaches the spherical f conversion you asked for, and cc-pVTZ is also the
smallest standard basis that drives the tight non-s path. Module-scoped fixtures
removed three duplicate calculations at the same time: 6 tests in 34 s, against
3 tests in 151 s before.

### Verification on this commit
